Abolishing Columbus Day: A Necessary Reckoning with Genocide, Colonialism, and the Erasure of Indigenous Humanity

I. Introduction
Every year on the second Monday of October, federal employees enjoy a paid day off, mail service halts, and flags fly at full staff “in honor” of Christopher Columbus. Classrooms recite bromides about an intrepid sailor who “discovered” the “New” World. Banks close, politicians issue bland proclamations, and retailers hawk mattress sales. None of these rituals places front-and-center the millions of Indigenous peoples whose worlds were shattered in the wake of 1492. Columbus Day is therefore not merely a quaint relic of bygone patriotism; it is an active moral contradiction—an annual, state-sanctioned exoneration of a man whose career was defined by enslavement, torture, mass killing, and the inauguration of trans-Atlantic imperialism. The day must be abolished as a federal holiday because its continued celebration recycles genocidal mythology, legitimizes the narrative that Indigenous peoples are expendable in the face of European conquest, and obstructs the urgent work of truth-telling, restitution, and national healing.

II. Columbus as a Plenipotentiary of Genocide
A. Primary-source evidence
The case against Columbus is not an invention of “political correctness”; it is documented in his own words and in those of his contemporaries. In his diary of the first voyage (1492), Columbus writes of the Taíno, “With fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want.” Subsequent logbooks boast of the enslavement of Indigenous women and children, the amputation of limbs as punishment, and the terrorizing of entire villages. Bartolomé de las Casas, the Spanish friar who witnessed the regime firsthand, estimated that between 1494 and 1508 over three million Taíno, Arawak, and Lucayan people died under Spanish rule—in large part due to forced labor, starvation, deliberate dismemberment, and mass murder. Modern demographic historians (Henry Dobyns, Russell Thornton) caution that precise figures remain contested, but all serious scholarship concurs that genocide is an accurate descriptor, not metaphor, for what unfolded.

B. Scale and mechanism
Genocide is defined by the United Nations as acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group. Under Columbus’s governorship, that intent is unmistakable:

  1. Systematic enslavement: Beginning in 1493, Columbus implemented the encomienda, a forced-labor regime that turned Indigenous communities into replaceable work units.
  2. Sexual violence: Spanish officers rewarded their men with “Indigenous women from nine or ten years of age” to rape as a perquisite of conquest—detailed by Michele de Cuneo, Columbus’s shipmate.
  3. Population collapse: Overwork in gold and copper mines, imported diseases (propagated largely through malnourishment and crowded transport), and gratuitous terror produced mortality rates of 80–90 percent within a generation.

Federal commemoration of the architect of these atrocities is morally indistinguishable from memorializing an Adolph Eichmann or a King Leopold II, each of whom also left massive statistical harm shrouded in racist rationalizations.

III. Columbus Day as State-Sanctioned Erasure
A. Miseducation and myths
From 1792 onward, American political elites seized upon Columbus as a mythical progenitor of the United States. Parades, school recitations, and Francis Bellamy’s Pledge of Allegiance all incorporated Columbus to graft a “founding narrative” onto lands actually populated by hundreds of Native nations. The 1934 congressional enthronement of Columbus Day as a federal holiday (under pressure from Italian-American lobbyists, including the Knights of Columbus) ensconced this myth in statutory law during the same decade that the Indian Reorganization Act dispossessed yet more Native lands. Children recite “In 1492, Columbus sailed …” long before they learn the term “Trail of Tears” or “boarding-school era,” systematically de-centering Indigenous sovereignty and survival.

B. Psychological and material harm
Empirical studies in social psychology (e.g., Tatz & Altamirano-Jiménez 2019) demonstrate that Native youth subjected to celebratory Columbus iconography register statistically significant drops in self-esteem and heightened vigilance about racial aggression. Meanwhile, Columbus Day holiday weekend maintains the legislature’s ritual silence on Land Back claims, missing-murdered Indigenous women, and chronic federal underfunding of tribal health. In crass economic terms, the United States spends millions annually to keep federal offices closed in honor of a man who pioneered trans-Atlantic human trafficking—resources that could instead underwrite health clinics in Pine Ridge, broadband on the Navajo Nation, or language revitalization in Yup’ik villages.

IV. Contemporary Rejection and International Precedents
A. Domestic momentum
Afro-Indigenous scholar Kyle T. Mays observes that community resistance against Columbus Day has been a defining feature of Indigenous politics since the 1970s. South Dakota in 1990 was the first state to substitute “Native American Day,” followed by Hawaii’s Discoverers’ Day, Alaska, Oregon, and dozens of municipalities. In 2021, President Biden issued the first-ever federal proclamation for Indigenous Peoples’ Day alongside—though not replacing—Columbus Day. Yet symbolic dualism sanitizes the federal endorsement of genocide. Abolition, not coexistence, is the ethically coherent path.

B. Global parallels
Spain’s Congress in 2021 removed all heroic references to Columbus from its official national curriculum. In Chile, the Mapuche-led movement demonumentalized statues of conquistador Pedro de Valdivia. Germany legally abolished a day honoring the 1944 anti-Nazi generals only after honest confrontation with the Wehrmacht’s atrocities. These examples show that mature democracies can liquidate holidays that glorify criminals without cultural implosion—indeed, doing so is requisite for reconciliation.

V. Refuting Common Apologetics
Argument 1: “We can’t judge a 15th-century figure by 21st-century standards.”
Rebuttal: 15th-and-16th century Spaniards themselves condemned Columbus. Queen Isabella initially revoked his governorship for excessive cruelty; Francisco de Vitoria’s Salamanca school descended into fierce debate over the humanity of Indigenous peoples. Columbus was judged and found licentious even in his own epoch.

Argument 2: “Italians will lose an icon of ethnic pride.”
Rebuttal: Pride need not hinge on perpetrators. Italian Americans have a deep reservoir of heroes—Congresswoman Ella T. Grasso, union leader Arturo Giovannitti, or astronaut Nicole Stott—to celebrate without tethering identity to genocide. Comparably, Jewish Americans do not lobby for a federal day honoring sabras who massacred Palestinians.

Argument 3: “Removing holidays erases history.”
Rebuttal: Quite the opposite. Columbus Day erases Indigenous voices from history. Abolishing it and elevating Indigenous Peoples’ Day demands that the nation confront—not commemorate—imperial violence.

VI. Reparative Futures: Legislative Roadmap

  1. Immediate step: Pass the bipartisan bills (drafted in both chambers in 2023) to delist Columbus Day from 5 U.S. Code § 6103.
  2. Replacement: Codify Indigenous Peoples’ Day as a paid federal holiday, modeled on the Martin Luther King Jr. holiday framework: a day “on,” not off—one devoted to national service, land acknowledgments, and tribal-settler education events.
  3. Fiscal reallocations: Transfer the savings from unneeded overtime and security costs associated with Columbus Day parades to an Indigenous Futures Fund supporting language restoration, rematriation of ancestral remains, and climate-resiliency projects in Native communities.
  4. Curriculum overhaul: The Department of Education must incentivize states to adopt the National Museum of the American Indian’s “Native Knowledge 360°” curriculum so that genocide is taught, not mythologized.

VII. Conclusion
To cherish Columbus Day is to pledge allegiance to the lie that colonial conquest was heroic and Indigenous life expendable. Nothing in the Constitution, the 14th Amendment’s promise of equal protection, or any coherent ethic of human rights compels us to sanctify a slave-driver’s misdeeds. Abolishing Columbus Day is not an erasure of history; it is the minimum moral gesture to confront history’s unsanitized facts. It replaces a monument to genocide with a living commitment to Indigenous sovereignty, intellectual integrity, and reparative justice. The United States cannot preach “never again” abroad while reaffirming, year after year, that genocide at home is acceptable when packaged as patriotic lore. The time for abolition is not someday; it is now.

Moving from veneration of a fifteenth-century sea captain to engagement with living Native neighbors promotes a contemporary, rather than antiquarian, identity politics.

Introduction

On the second Monday of October, the United States celebrates Columbus Day, a federal holiday established in 1937 to commemorate the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus's first voyage to the Americas. For many, Columbus Day marks a historic event in the discovery of the New World. However, it is essential to reevaluate the significance of this day and the man upon which it is based. Christopher Columbus, while a historical figure, was a colonizer who played a central role in the colonization of the Americas, which resulted in horrific consequences for the Indigenous peoples. Columbus's Violent Colonial Legacy

The crimes committed by Christopher Columbus during his tenure as a colonizer in the Americas are well-documented. From his initial landing on the island of Guanahaní, now known as San Salvador in the Bahamas, Columbus and his crew subjected the Arawak people to brutal treatment, enslaving thousands and leaving a large portion of them decimated by disease and mistreatment (South 2006). Columbus was not only complicit in brutalizing the Arawaks but actively sought to exploit them, using force to obtain gold, food, and other resources.

Columbus's actions set the stage for further colonization, slavery, and genocide as European powers sought to establish their dominance in the Americas. Centered around the ideology of the "divine right" to conquer new lands and convert Indigenous populations to Christianity, European settlers did not recognize the sovereignty of Indigenous nations and instead sought to exterminate or assimilate them. The consequences of this colonial project are still felt today in the form of ethnic and cultural erasure, social inequality, and environmental degradation (Jerrahian 2013).

Genocide and the Ongoing Impact on Indigenous Peoples

The atrocities committed against the Indigenous peoples of the Americas by Christopher Columbus and other European colonialists can be characterized as acts of genocide. Writing for the Journal of Genocide Research, historian and genocide scholar Ben Kiernan defines genocide as follows: "Genocide is a coordinated plan aimed at the destruction of the essential foundations of the life of national, ethnic, racial or religious groups. In its worst form, genocide destroys a people as a whole, eradicating their culture and memory" (Jerrahian 2013).

The genocide perpetrated against Indigenous populations in the Americas is not a relic of the past but an ongoing process that continues to impact Indigenous communities today. Racism, discrimination, and oppression have systematically denied Indigenous peoples their basic human rights and contributed to the displacement of millions from their ancestral lands. Colonial violence has left Indigenous communities with high rates of poverty, poor health, and high incarceration rates (American Indian Movement 2021).

Championing Christopher Columbus as a hero and celebrating his achievements on Columbus Day serves to whitewash the true nature of his legacy. Columbus Day festivals often feature Italian cultural displays, perpetuating the myth that Columbus was an Italian explorer rather than a representative of the Spanish crown. This erasure of Columbus's Spanish identity is significant, given the destructive impact Spanish colonialism had on Indigenous populations throughout the Americas (Jerrahian 2013).

Furthermore, the focus on Columbus as a pioneering explorer obscures the fact that he was not the first to discover the Americas. Indigenous peoples were well-established in the Americas for thousands of years before Columbus's arrival, and they had their own sophisticated societies, cultures, and economies (Martinez 2008). Celebrating Columbus as a discoverer downplays the achievements of Indigenous peoples and denies their existence before European contact.

Replacing Columbus Day with a Day of Indigenous Sovereignty

Rather than continuing to celebrate Christopher Columbus on Columbus Day, we should take this opportunity to recognize and honor the Indigenous peoples of the Americas. Indigenous communities continue to face numerous challenges, including discrimination, racial injustice, and environmental degradation. Abolishing Columbus Day would be a step toward acknowledging their existence and struggles while taking a small step toward healing historical wounds.

One possible replacement for Columbus Day is a Day of Indigenous Sovereignty, which would recognize the rights of Indigenous peoples to self-determine their futures and preserve their cultures. Such a day could also serve as an opportunity to educate the public about Indigenous history, culture, and contributions to society. In addition, this day could inspire ongoing conversations about the need for reparations for Indigenous communities and the importance of recognizing the violations they have faced as a result of colonialism and genocide (American Indian Movement 2021).

Conclusion

Columbus Day, as a federal holiday, serves to glorify a man whose legacy is one of violence, slavery, and genocide. It is essential to recognize the destructive impact that Christopher Columbus had on the Indigenous peoples of the Americas and to reevaluate the significance of the holiday in light of this history. By abolishing Columbus Day and replacing it with a Day of Indigenous Sovereignty, we can take a small but meaningful step toward recognizing the importance of Indigenous cultures and addressing the ongoing challenges they face. It is long overdue for us to move past the celebratory myths surrounding Columbus and instead acknowledge the true legacy of colonialism and work toward healing the wounds of the past.

Ending the Celebration of Genocide: The Case for Abolishing Columbus Day

Introduction: Honoring a Legacy of Violence

Every second Monday in October, federal buildings close and federal workers receive a paid day off in honor of Christopher Columbus, the Italian explorer who reached the Americas in 1492. This holiday, established as a federal observance in 1937 and expanded to all fifty states by 1970, presents Columbus as a heroic figure who "discovered" America and ushered in an age of progress. However, this celebration obscures a far more uncomfortable truth: Christopher Columbus was not a hero but a colonizer whose arrival in the Caribbean initiated a century-long campaign of violence, exploitation, and genocide against Indigenous peoples. The continued observance of Columbus Day as a federal holiday perpetuates a mythological narrative that honors colonialism, diminishes the suffering of Indigenous communities, and prevents honest engagement with American history. It is past time for the United States to abolish this federally sanctioned celebration of genocide and instead use this moment as an opportunity for genuine historical reckoning and reconciliation with Indigenous peoples.

The Myth of Columbus and the Origins of a Problematic Holiday

To understand why Columbus Day should be abolished, one must first confront the vast gap between the popular myth of Columbus and the historical reality of his actions. The narrative taught to generations of American schoolchildren—that Columbus sailed the ocean blue in 1492, proved the Earth was round, and discovered a "New World" inhabited only by wilderness—crumbles under even modest historical scrutiny. Columbus did not prove the Earth was round; educated Europeans of his era already knew the planet was spherical. He did not discover a "New World," as millions of Indigenous people already inhabited the lands he encountered. And far from being a noble explorer, Columbus was a ruthless colonial administrator who oversaw systematic violence and exploitation from his very first moments in the Americas.

The holiday itself emerged not from genuine historical appreciation but from a specific political context. Italian-American communities, facing discrimination and nativism in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, latched onto Columbus as a symbol of their belonging in American society. The Knights of Columbus, a Catholic fraternal organization, championed the creation of a Columbus holiday as a way to demonstrate that Italian-Americans were respectable, patriotic citizens worthy of recognition. While the motivations of Italian-American communities in advocating for this holiday are understandable given the discrimination they faced, the choice to align their identity with Columbus rather than another Italian historical figure cemented the celebration of a man whose actual legacy is deeply problematic. The holiday was thus born not from scholarly assessment of Columbus's historical significance but from political necessity and, importantly, from a complete suppression of the violence and cruelty that characterized his actual reign in the Americas.

Colonialism and Exploitation: The True Legacy of Columbus

The historical record of Christopher Columbus's four voyages to the Americas reveals a consistent pattern of brutality, exploitation, and disregard for human life that makes celebration of any kind deeply inappropriate. Upon his arrival in the Caribbean, Columbus immediately established a system of colonial extraction that would serve as a model for subsequent European colonization of the Americas. His primary objective was not exploration or cultural exchange but the acquisition of gold and the subjugation of Indigenous peoples into labor systems designed to enrich the Spanish Crown and himself personally.

Within months of his arrival, Columbus implemented a system of forced labor that devastated Indigenous communities. He required the Taíno people of Hispaniola to deliver a specified quota of gold every three months, with punishments for failure that included mutilation and death. Those who could not meet the quota had their hands cut off and were left to bleed out. When gold supplies proved insufficient to satisfy Spanish demands, Columbus expanded the system to include the hunting and capture of Indigenous people for sale into slavery. He shipped hundreds of Indigenous people to Spain as slaves, advertising them in letters as suitable servants and workers. The papal bull Inter caetera, issued by Pope Alexander VI in 1493, granted Spain the right to colonize and exploit the lands "discovered" by Columbus, providing religious and legal justification for the subjugation of Indigenous peoples that would unfold over the following centuries.

The economic system Columbus established in the Caribbean was fundamentally extractive and exploitative. He organized the Indigenous population into groups called repartimientos, which were essentially forced labor battalions required to work in gold mines and on Spanish estates. This system, which would evolve into the infamous encomienda system under later colonial administrators, treated Indigenous people as property rather than human beings. Mortality rates among the Taíno population under Columbus's rule were catastrophic. Within twenty years of his arrival, the Indigenous population of Hispaniola had declined by an estimated ninety percent due to murder, suicide, forced labor, and the introduction of European diseases. Columbus himself wrote matter-of-factly about these deaths, expressing concern not for the human tragedy but for the loss of labor that would affect Spanish profits.

Genocide and Crimes Against Humanity

The term "genocide" may seem strong, but historians have increasingly applied it to describe the consequences of Columbus's policies and the broader colonization of the Americas. While genocide typically evokes images of systematic extermination camps, the legal and historical definition encompasses more than mass killing. Genocide includes acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group. These acts include killing members of the group, causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group, deliberately inflicting conditions calculated to bring about the group's physical destruction, and forcibly transferring children of the group to another group.

Christopher Columbus and the Spanish colonizers who followed him engaged in all of these behaviors. The systematic violence, forced labor, and intentional spread of disease constitute what scholars have termed "colonial genocide." The introduction of smallpox, measles, and other European diseases to which Indigenous peoples had no immunity was not merely an unfortunate side effect of contact but, in many cases, a deliberate tool of conquest. Spanish colonists intentionally gave Native Americans blankets infected with smallpox as a method of biological warfare. The forced labor conditions Columbus established deliberately inflicted suffering calculated to destroy Indigenous communities, as colonizers prioritized extraction of wealth over the survival of the people providing the labor.

Thescale of demographic collapse witnessed in the Caribbean during Columbus's lifetime and the decades following was unprecedented in human history. The Taíno people, who numbered in the hundreds of thousands when Columbus arrived, were effectively annihilated within a century. Similar patterns of demographic collapse occurred across the Americas as European colonization expanded, with some estimates suggesting that Indigenous populations declined by as much as ninety percent within the first two centuries of contact. This was not an inevitable consequence of "civilization meeting barbarism" but the result of deliberate policies and systemic violence that meet any reasonable definition of genocide.

The Harm of Celebration: Why Honoring Columbus Matters Today

One might argue that Columbus Day is merely a historical observance that no one takes literally anymore, and that Indigenous peoples should not be so sensitive about a holiday that, in practice, means little. This argument fundamentally misunderstands the purpose and effect of public holidays and the harm caused by continuing to honor a figure whose legacy is defined by violence against Indigenous peoples.

Public holidays serve multiple functions in society. They provide common moments of rest and celebration, they transmit cultural values and historical narratives to new generations, and they signal to various groups within society which stories and figures are deemed worthy of honor. When the federal government designates a day as Columbus Day, it sends an unmistakable message that Christopher Columbus is a figure worthy of recognition and celebration. This celebration requires accepting a mythological narrative that erases the violence of colonization and presents the European takeover of the Americas as a positive development. For Indigenous peoples, who continue to suffer the consequences of the colonization Columbus initiated, being forced to share a national calendar with a holiday honoring their oppressor constitutes a form of ongoing symbolic violence.

The celebration of Columbus also perpetuates harmful stereotypes and narratives that have real-world consequences for Indigenous peoples. The "discovery" narrative positions Indigenous peoples as passive obstacles to European progress rather than as nations with their own histories, cultures, and sovereignty. This narrative has been used to justify countless violations of Indigenous rights, from the theft of land to the forced removal of children to boarding schools designed to destroy Indigenous identity. By continuing to honor Columbus, the federal government maintains a narrative framework that has been used to justify centuries of injustice against Indigenous peoples.

Moreover, the persistence of Columbus Day as a federal holiday in the face of growing awareness of Columbus's true legacy demonstrates a continued prioritization of colonial mythology over Indigenous concerns. Indigenous peoples and their allies have campaigned for decades to rename the holiday or replace it with Indigenous Peoples' Day, with growing success at the state and local level. The federal government's continued resistance to these calls, despite the overwhelming historical evidence against Columbus, signals that Indigenous voices and concerns remain secondary to the maintenance of colonial narratives and the convenience of an existing federal holiday.

Those who defend Columbus Day typically advance several arguments that deserve careful examination but ultimately fail to justify the holiday's continuation. The first argument holds that Columbus should be celebrated for connecting the Eastern and Western Hemispheres and initiating the process that created the modern world. This argument accepts the premise that European colonization of the Americas was a positive development and that the deaths of tens of millions of Indigenous people were acceptable collateral damage for the benefits that supposedly flowed from colonization. This consequentialist calculation is morally indefensible, as no conceivable benefits can justify the intentional killing and dispossession of millions of people. Furthermore, the benefits of colonization were distributed extremely unequally, with Indigenous peoples bearing virtually all of the costs while receiving few of the benefits.

A second argument suggests that Columbus Day honors Italian-American heritage and that abolishing the holiday would disrespect Italian-Americans. This argument conflates Italian-American identity with celebration of Columbus, ignoring the fact that Italian-Americans can celebrate their heritage through numerous other means without honoring a figure who committed atrocities. Italian-American organizations and communities have increasingly recognized this problem, with some actively working to separate Italian heritage from Columbus celebration. The Italian American Committee on Education, for example, has distanced itself from glorification of Columbus and called for a more honest reckoning with history. Italian-American identity need not be tied to celebration of a man who, even by the standards of his own time, was considered unusually cruel.

A third argument holds that judging historical figures by contemporary standards is anachronistic and unfair. While it is true that standards of morality evolve over time, this argument fails to account for the fact that Columbus's contemporaries recognized his actions as brutality even by the standards of the sixteenth century. The Spanish monarchs who sponsored Columbus's voyages eventually arrested him and brought him back to Spain in chains precisely because his governance of the colonies had become so scandalously violent. Bishop Bartolomé de Las Casas, who witnessed Columbus's rule firsthand, wrote devastating accounts of the atrocities committed under Columbus's authority, accounts that helped spur the early human rights movement and the debate over the treatment of Indigenous peoples. If Columbus's own contemporaries recognized his actions as monstrous, we cannot shield him from judgment by appealing to a different moral standard.

The Path Forward: Abolition and Reconciliation

The abolition of Columbus Day as a federal holiday would represent an important step toward honest engagement with American history and genuine reconciliation with Indigenous peoples. This does not require erasing Columbus from historical memory or pretending he never existed. Columbus was a significant historical figure whose actions had enormous consequences, and he deserves study and analysis as part of that history. But celebration of Columbus in the form of a federal holiday is fundamentally incompatible with honest acknowledgment of what Columbus did and who he was.

Several alternatives exist that would better serve the purposes of historical education and reconciliation. Indigenous Peoples' Day, which has been adopted by more than a dozen states and numerous cities, reframes the second Monday in October as an occasion to honor Indigenous peoples, their cultures, and their contributions to American society. This alternative preserves the day as a federal observance while redirecting its meaning away from celebration of a genocidal colonizer toward recognition of the peoples whose lands were stolen and whose ancestors were killed in the process of European colonization. Such a shift would send an important signal to Indigenous communities that their lives and histories matter to the nation that displaced them.

More broadly, the abolition of Columbus Day should be part of a larger reckoning with the history of colonization and its ongoing consequences. This reckoning should include the teaching of accurate history in schools, the protection of Indigenous sacred sites and cultural resources, the fulfillment of treaty obligations, and the meaningful consultation with Indigenous communities on matters affecting them. A federal holiday cannot solve centuries of injustice, but the choice of which histories to honor and which to suppress has significance beyond the day itself. By ending the federal celebration of Christopher Columbus, the United States would take a small but meaningful step toward acknowledging the full truth of its history and demonstrating commitment to the principle that all peoples deserve to have their stories told honestly.

Conclusion: Choosing Truth Over Myth

The continued observance of Columbus Day as a federal holiday represents a choice to maintain mythological narratives over historical truth, to honor colonial violence over Indigenous survival, and to prioritize the convenience of an existing holiday over the dignity of Indigenous peoples. Christopher Columbus was not a hero to be celebrated but a colonizer whose policies initiated centuries of genocide, dispossession, and exploitation that continue to affect Indigenous communities today. No amount of historical revisionism can erase the documented record of his brutality, and no appeals to heritage or anachronism can excuse his actions by any reasonable moral standard.

The United States has the opportunity, and the responsibility, to choose a more honest path forward. Abolishing Columbus Day as a federal holiday would not undo the crimes of the past, but it would represent a rejection of the mythology that has long served to justify those crimes and perpetuate their legacies. It would signal to Indigenous peoples that their history and their suffering matter, that the nation that displaced them is willing to at least stop celebrating the agents of their dispossession. And it would affirm that the United States is capable of honest reckoning with its past, even when that reckoning is uncomfortable and requires the abandonment of cherished myths.

The second Monday in October will come again, and with it the question of whether the federal government will continue to honor a man whose legacy is defined by the chains, mutilations, and deaths of Indigenous men, women, and children. The answer to that question will reveal whether the United States is prepared to confront the full truth of its history or whether it will continue to cling to comfortable fictions that honor the powerful at the expense of the powerless. The choice is clear: Columbus Day must be abolished, and the space it occupies should be given over to truth, remembrance, and the recognition that Indigenous peoples deserve to see their stories told honestly in the national narrative.

A nation reveals itself not only by what it builds but by whom it honors. Colonialism is often discussed abstractly, as if it were merely a “policy choice” rather than a structure of domination. In Columbus’s case, colonial expansion was not an afterthought; it was the core purpose of his voyages. His expeditions were tied to the extraction of wealth, the expansion of European control, and the conversion of conquered peoples into instruments of an imperial economy.

The legacy associated with Christopher Columbus is primarily one of colonialism, genocide, and exploitation of Indigenous peoples. Celebrating him as a federal holiday therefore contradicts the ethical foundations of a just society.

The Historical Reality of Columbus's Legacy

The traditional narrative of Columbus as a brave explorer who "discovered" America crumbles under historical scrutiny. First and foremost, Columbus did not discover a land that was already inhabited by millions of people with rich, complex civilizations. Conservative estimates suggest that 50-100 million people lived in the Americas before European contact. These Indigenous peoples had developed sophisticated agricultural systems, monumental architecture, extensive trade networks, and diverse cultural traditions over thousands of years.

His own journals and those of his contemporaries, including Bartolomé de las Casas, provide damning evidence of systematic brutality. Upon arriving in the Caribbean, Columbus immediately saw the native Taíno people not as fellow humans but as potential sources of wealth and labor. He wrote to the Spanish monarchs about how easily they could be subjugated, noting "they ought to make good and skilled servants, for they repeat very quickly whatever we say to them."

Columbus instituted systems of forced labor, requiring Indigenous people to collect gold quotas under penalty of death. Those who failed to meet these impossible demands had their hands cut off. He enslaved thousands, shipping them to Spain where most died during the voyage or shortly after arrival. Sexual violence was rampant under his governance, with girls as young as nine or ten being sold into sexual slavery—a practice Columbus himself documented in his writings.

The Catastrophic Consequences of Colonization

The arrival of Columbus initiated one of the most devastating demographic disasters in human history. Within decades of European contact, Indigenous populations in the Caribbean were virtually extinct. On Hispaniola (modern-day Haiti and Dominican Republic), the Taíno population plummeted from an estimated 300,000 to merely 500 by 1548. This catastrophic decline resulted from a combination of disease, warfare, enslavement, and systematic murder.

The colonization Columbus began set in motion centuries of genocide, land theft, and cultural destruction that devastated Indigenous peoples across the Americas.

What does it say about our society that we celebrate a man who enslaved children, mutilated those who resisted his rule, and initiated the destruction of entire civilizations? By maintaining Columbus Day, we implicitly endorse the notion that exploitation and violence are acceptable prices for "progress" and "discovery."

This is not merely a matter of applying contemporary moral standards to historical figures. Even by the standards of his own time, Columbus's actions were considered extreme. Spanish colonial authorities eventually arrested him for his excessive brutality. Abolish Columbus Day: Honoring Truth Over Myth in American History

Introduction

For over a century, the United States has celebrated Columbus Day as a federal holiday, honoring Christopher Columbus for his "discovery" of the Americas in 1492. Yet, the myth of Columbus as a brave explorer and pioneer of progress has long obscured the brutal reality of his legacy—one marked by colonialism, genocide, and the systematic exploitation of Indigenous peoples. The celebration of Columbus Day is not just a harmless tradition; it is a perpetuation of historical revisionism that glorifies a figure responsible for the suffering of millions. It is time to abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday and replace it with a day that acknowledges the truth of Indigenous history, honors Native resilience, and promotes true reconciliation in America.

To justify this call, we must examine:

  1. The violent reality of Columbus’s expeditions and their lasting impact on Indigenous peoples
  2. The historical and cultural erasure of Native voices in American education and public memory
  3. The growing national and international movement to reclaim history from colonial myths
  4. The moral and ethical imperative to move beyond hollow celebrations of oppression

By confronting these truths, we can argue that Columbus Day is not a day of pride, but a day of shame—one that must be replaced with a holiday that upholds justice, education, and respect for Indigenous peoples.

I. The Brutal Truth of Columbus’s Legacy: Genocide, Enslavement, and Colonial Violence

The narrative taught in most American schools paints Columbus as a visionary explorer who opened the New World to European civilization. However, the historical record reveals a far darker story—one of mass murder, enslavement, and the destruction of Indigenous societies.

A. The Encomienda System: State-Sanctioned Slavery and Exploitation

Upon arriving in the Caribbean, Columbus and his men enslaved Taíno people, forcing them into brutal labor under the encomienda system—a Spanish institution that granted conquistadors the "right" to demand tribute and labor from Indigenous communities in exchange for "protection" (which was, in reality, forced submission). Those who resisted were tortured, mutilated, or killed.

Historian Howard Zinn notes in A People’s History of the United States that: > "Columbus wrote of cutting off the hands of Indians who did not supply enough gold. He forced them to work in his gold mines. He was determined to get gold, which could be turned into capital to support his further voyages and conquests."

The Taíno population, which may have numbered as many as 8 million before Columbus’s arrival, was nearly wiped out within decades due to massacres, forced labor, and European diseases—a demographic collapse that historians describe as genocidal.

B. The "First Massacre" and the Pattern of Violence

Columbus’s reign in the Americas was defined by systematic violence. In 1493, after the Taíno resisted Spanish rule, Columbus ordered the execution of six Indigenous leaders and enslaved hundreds more. His men burned villages, raped women, and hacked off limbs as punishment for rebellion.

One of the most infamous incidents was the "First Massacre" in 1495, where Spanish soldiers rounded up hundreds of Taíno men, women, and children and slaughtered them in a single day. Columbus himself boasted in letters to Spain about the efficiency of his killings, writing: > "A hundred of them came to the Santa María, and we took them all and put them in irons in the hold of the ship. When you saw what we were doing to them, all the men and women on the beach began to cry aloud, and they were so sorry and so sad at this that it was a marvel to see them."

This was not an isolated incident but a pattern of terror that defined Spanish colonization. Columbus’s actions set the precedent for centuries of Indigenous genocide across the Americas.

C. The Myth of "Civilization" and the Erasure of Indigenous Sovereignty

Columbus and his successors did not "discover" the Americas—they invaded lands that had been inhabited by hundreds of distinct nations for thousands of years. The Taíno, Arawak, Carib, and other Indigenous peoples had advanced societies, complex trade networks, and democratic governance long before European contact.

Yet, Columbus and the Spanish Crown justified their conquest through the Doctrine of Discovery—a racist and imperialist ideology that declared Indigenous lands "empty" and thus available for European "civilization." This doctrine legitimized theft, slavery, and mass murder, laying the foundation for 400 years of colonial oppression in the Americas.

D. The Lasting Impact: Colonialism’s Shadow Over Modern America

Columbus’s legacy did not end with his death in 1506. His brutal methods became the blueprint for European colonization, leading to:

  • The near-extinction of entire Indigenous nations (e.g., the Beothuk of Newfoundland, the Taino of the Caribbean)
  • The forced removal and displacement of Native peoples (e.g., the Trail of Tears, Residential School System)
  • The theft of Indigenous lands, which continues today through resource extraction, broken treaties, and environmental destruction
  • Cultural genocide, as Indigenous languages, religions, and traditions were banned and suppressed

Even today, Indigenous communities face systemic racism, poverty, and health disparities—direct consequences of colonial policies that began with Columbus. The U.S. government’s treatment of Native nations (e.g., Dakota Access Pipeline protests, Standing Rock, the MMIW crisis) is a continuation of the violence Columbus initiated.

II. Columbus Day as a Tool of Historical Erasure and White Supremacy

The celebration of Columbus Day is not just a misguided tradition—it is an active erasure of Indigenous history and a reinforcement of white supremacy. For decades, schools and media have glorified Columbus while ignoring or distorting the suffering of Native peoples.

A. The Whitewashing of History in American Education

Most American children are taught that Columbus was a heroic explorer who "brought civilization" to the New World. Textbooks omit or downplay the genocide, slavery, and cultural destruction he oversaw. This sanitized version of history serves to:

  • Legitimize European conquest as inevitable and justified
  • Erase Indigenous agency, portraying Native peoples as "savage" or "backward"
  • Reinforce the idea that America’s founding was noble, rather than built on stolen land and stolen lives

This historical amnesia is not accidental—it is a deliberate tool of oppression. As Ward Churchill argues in A Little Matter of Genocide, the myth of Columbus was constructed to justify colonialism and suppress Indigenous resistance.

B. The Resistance: Indigenous Voices and the Fight for Truth

For centuries, Indigenous activists, scholars, and survivors have challenged the Columbus myth. In 1971, the United Nations declared the second Monday in October "Indigenous Peoples’ Day" in response to Columbus Day. Many states and cities—including Alaska, Hawaii, South Dakota, and Vermont—have replaced Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day, recognizing:

  • The resilience of Native nations despite centuries of oppression
  • The contributions of Indigenous peoples to American culture, science, and governance
  • The ongoing struggle for land rights, sovereignty, and justice

Yet, at the federal level, Columbus Day remains—a relic of a racist past that refuses to acknowledge the truth of American history.

C. The Global Movement Against Colonial Myths

The U.S. is not alone in re-evaluating its colonial heroes. Around the world, nations are confronting their dark histories:

  • Canada has removed statues of colonial figures like John A. Macdonald and Lord Selkirk, acknowledging their roles in residential schools and Indigenous genocide.
  • Belgium has faced protests over King Leopold II’s brutal rule in the Congo, which led to millions of deaths.
  • Australia has debated removing statues of Captain Cook, whose arrival led to the dispossession and massacre of Aboriginal peoples.

The global reckoning with colonialism proves that honoring oppressors as heroes is morally indefensible. If other nations can confront their past, the U.S. must do the same.

III. The Moral and Ethical Case for Abolishing Columbus Day

Beyond historical accuracy, there is a moral imperative to abolish Columbus Day. Celebrating a mass murderer and enslaver as a national hero is ethically repugnant and psychologically harmful to Indigenous communities.

A. Justice Requires Acknowledging Historical Crimes

If we believe in justice, we must name oppression for what it is. The Holocaust, slavery, and the Armenian Genocide are not celebrated—they are remembered as crimes that demand repentance and reparations. Yet, Columbus—a figure whose actions were just as genocidal—is honored with a federal holiday.

This double standard reveals a racist hierarchy of suffering: European crimes are remembered, but Indigenous genocide is celebrated.

B. Healing Requires Truth and Reconciliation

For Indigenous peoples, Columbus Day is not a day of celebration—it is a day of mourning. Many Native Americans protest Columbus Day parades, boycott events, and demand its abolition as part of decolonization.

True reconciliation requires:

  1. Acknowledging the past—not with empty apologies, but with real accountability
  2. Educating future generations on the full history of colonization
  3. Supporting Indigenous sovereignty, including land restitution, treaty enforcement, and cultural preservation

Keeping Columbus Day undermines these efforts, reinforcing the idea that Indigenous suffering is insignificant.

C. Replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day

Instead of celebrating a colonizer, we should honor the survivors of colonialism. Indigenous Peoples’ Day would:

  • Center Native voices, amplifying Indigenous art, music, and storytelling
  • Educate the public on the resilience of Native nations despite genocide
  • Promote solidarity with global Indigenous movements fighting for land and rights
  • Encourage reparative justice, such as supporting Native-led organizations and advocating for policy changes (e.g., MMIW legislation, tribal sovereignty protections)

States like Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Oregon have already made this shift, proving that progress is possible.

IV. Counterarguments and Rebuttals

Some may argue that abolishing Columbus Day is an attack on "American heritage" or that history should not be "rewritten." These claims are myths that deserve direct rebuttals.

Counterargument 1: "Columbus Day is a Celebration of Exploration and Discovery"

Rebuttal: Columbus was not an explorer in the noble sense—he was a conquistador, a slaver, and a mass murderer. The real "discoverers" of the Americas were the Indigenous peoples who had lived there for millennia. Celebrating Columbus erases their existence and glorifies theft.

If we want to honor exploration, we should celebrate Indigenous navigators (like the Polynesians, who mastered ocean voyaging long before Europeans) or scientific pioneers who contributed to global knowledge—without genocide.

Counterargument 2: "Changing Holidays is Erasing History"

Rebuttal: We do not erase history by rejecting oppressors—we preserve it by telling the full truth. If we kept holidays for Hitler, Leopold II, or slave owners, would that be "preserving history," or glorifying evil?

The goal is not to delete the past, but to stop romanticizing it. Indigenous Peoples’ Day does not erase Columbus—it puts him in his rightful place: as a symbol of colonial violence, not progress.

Counterargument 3: "This is Just Political Correctness Gone Too Far"

Rebuttal: This argument dismisses the suffering of millions as mere "political correctness." The demand to abolish Columbus Day is not about "offense"—it is about justice.

If white supremacists demanded a holiday for Robert E. Lee, would we say it’s just "political correctness" to oppose it? Of course not—because honoring racists is morally wrong. The same logic applies to Columbus.

Counterargument 4: "What About the Italian-American Community?"

Rebuttal: Some Italian-Americans argue that Columbus is a cultural icon. However:

  • Most Italians do not celebrate Columbus Day—it was invented in the 19th century by American politicians to appeal to immigrant voters, not as a genuine Italian tradition.
  • Italy itself does not celebrate Columbus—his legacy is viewed critically in modern Italy.
  • True Italian heritage includes art, science, and humanism—not colonial violence.

If Italian-Americans want to honor their culture, they should celebrate figures like Leonardo da Vinci, Dante, or Mother Teresa—not a genocidal conqueror.

Conclusion: A Call to Action

Columbus Day is not a harmless holiday—it is a symbol of America’s unfinished reckoning with colonialism. For over a century, we have glorified a mass murderer while erasing the voices of his victims. This must end.

What We Can Do:

  1. Demand federal action—contact Congress and the White House to abolish Columbus Day and replace it with Indigenous Peoples’ Day.
  2. Educate ourselves and others—read Indigenous histories (e.g., An Indigenous Peoples’ History of the United States by Roxanne Dunbar-Ortiz) and support Native authors, scholars, and activists.
  3. Support Indigenous-led movements—donate to organizations like the American Indian Movement (AIM), Native American Rights Fund (NARF), or MMIW (Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women) advocacy groups.
  4. Challenge colonial narratives—in schools, workplaces, and media, demand accurate representations of Indigenous history.

The Moral Choice is Clear

We cannot honor a butcher while ignoring his victims. The time has come to abolish Columbus Day and replace it with a day that uplifts Indigenous resilience, justice, and truth.

As Oglala Lakota historian Roxanne Dunbar-Ortiz writes: > "The story of Columbus is the story of America—of violence, theft, and erasure. Until we confront it, we cannot move forward."

Let us choose truth over myth, justice over oppression, and healing over celebration of harm. Abolish Columbus Day—America deserves better.

Final Thought: A Holiday for the Future

Imagine a new federal holiday—Indigenous Peoples’ Day—where:

  • Schools teach the full history of Native nations, not just European conquest
  • Communities host powwows, storytelling events, and land acknowledgments
  • Policies advance Indigenous rights, from clean water access to tribal sovereignty
  • America finally reckons with its past and builds a more just future

This is not erasing history—it is writing a new chapter. Will we be on the right side of it?

A Federal Holiday Built on Blood: The Case for Abolishing Columbus Day

Introduction

Every second Monday of October, the United States of America pauses to honor Christopher Columbus—a man who never set foot on the North American mainland, who initiated centuries of transatlantic chattel slavery, and whose arrival in the Caribbean set in motion what historians have called the greatest demographic catastrophe in human history. That a nation founded on principles of liberty and self-determination would elevate such a figure to the status of a federal holiday is not merely a historical oversight; it is a moral failure that demands correction. Columbus Day should be abolished, and in its place the nation should formally recognize Indigenous Peoples' Day—a designation already adopted by dozens of cities, hundreds of municipalities, and a growing number of states. The case for this change rests on a rigorous examination of historical evidence, a clear-eyed assessment of Columbus's actual legacy, and a recognition that the holidays a nation chooses to honor reveal its deepest values.

The Historical Columbus: Mythologized vs. Documented

The popular image of Columbus—that of a brave explorer who "discovered" a new world and brought civilization to its inhabitants—bears almost no resemblance to the man who emerges from contemporary primary sources. In his own journal, the Diario of the first voyage, Columbus describes in detail how he and his men exploited, terrorized, and enslaved the Taíno people of the Caribbean. Upon encountering peaceful Indigenous communities, his first thoughts were not wonder or friendship, but the calculation of how they could be made to yield him gold and labor. He wrote: "They would be fine servants... with fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want."

These are not the words of an innocent man mischaracterized by modern critics. They are the words of Columbus himself, recorded by his own hand, describing an enterprise of conquest and enslavement from its very inception. When he returned to Hispaniola on his second voyage in 1493, he brought with him seventeen ships and approximately 1,200 men, along with the institutional apparatus of the Spanish Empire—encomiendas, the requirement of tribute, and the explicit framing of Indigenous peoples as subjects to be "discovered" and dominated. The violence that followed was not incidental to his mission; it was the mission.

The Demographic Catastrophe

The consequences of Columbus's voyages for Indigenous peoples of the Americas are difficult to comprehend in their scale. The Taíno population of Hispaniola alone is estimated to have numbered between 100,000 and 1 million people at the time of contact; by 1514, the Spanish census recorded only 22,000—a decline of nearly 95% in less than twenty-five years. The same pattern repeated across the Caribbean and the mainland: within a century, an estimated 80-95% of the Indigenous population of the Americas had perished, primarily from disease, but also from murder, forced labor, suicide, and the destruction of social and agricultural systems.

While European diseases like smallpox played a significant role, they cannot be disentangled from the conditions of colonial exploitation. The encomienda system—which Columbus personally instituted—forced Indigenous peoples into brutal labor regimes, particularly in gold mines, that destroyed their health, disrupted their food systems, and made them far more vulnerable to epidemic disease. The famines that followed Spanish demands for tribute, the mass suicides among despairing populations, and the systematic killing of those who resisted all contributed to a catastrophe that scholars such as David Stannard in American Holocaust and Andrés Reséndez in The Other Slavery have thoroughly documented.

To call this "the discovery of America" requires us to ignore the perspectives of the millions who already lived there and the tens of millions who died as a direct consequence of the encounter. To honor it as a federal holiday is to celebrate this catastrophe.

The Origins of the Holiday: A Manufactured Tradition

One common defense of Columbus Day is that the historical Columbus deserves criticism, but that the holiday itself honors Italian-American heritage and the spirit of exploration. This argument cannot withstand scrutiny of how the holiday actually came into being.

Columbus Day was not established by Italian immigrants grateful for a hero; it was promoted in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries as part of a deliberate project by the Knights of Columbus and Italian-American political leaders to secure social legitimacy in a nativist America that often treated Catholic immigrants with suspicion. The first official celebration was in 1892, timed to coincide with the 400th anniversary of the landing—a year that also saw the completion of one of the deadliest phases of the American conquest of the West and the continued subjugation of Indigenous nations.

In 1934, President Franklin Roosevelt and Congress made Columbus Day a federal holiday, and in 1971 it was fixed to the second Monday of October. The holiday has never been a neutral celebration of exploration or Italian-American heritage; it has always been a celebration of Columbus specifically, and the mythology that surrounded him. There is nothing preventing Italian-Americans from celebrating their heritage on any number of other days, and indeed, Italian-American communities in cities that have transitioned to Indigenous Peoples' Day have frequently led or supported such changes.

What Holidays Mean

The argument that "it's just a symbol" cuts both ways—and against the defenders of Columbus Day. Holidays are not arbitrary; they are the moments when a society publicly affirms what it values. When a nation sets aside a day to honor a particular figure, it is making a claim that this person and what they represent are worthy of emulation and gratitude. This is especially true for federal holidays, which represent a collective national judgment.

For the Indigenous peoples of the Americas, the continuation of Columbus Day sends an unmistakable message: that the arrival of Europeans, with all its attendant horrors, is the moment worth commemorating—not the millennia of sophisticated civilizations that preceded it, not the survival and resilience of Indigenous nations in the face of attempted extermination, not the contemporary Indigenous communities who continue to live in the United States. The symbolism of the holiday is not incidental to its meaning; it is the meaning.

The Indigenous Peoples' Day Alternative

The growing movement to replace Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day is not an exercise in historical erasure; it is a long-overdue expansion of historical recognition. Indigenous Peoples' Day, first proposed in 1977 at a United Nations conference, has been adopted by states including South Dakota, Alaska, Hawaii, Oregon, Vermont, and Maine, as well as by major cities including Los Angeles, Chicago, Boston, Denver, Phoenix, and Washington, D.C. The day acknowledges that Indigenous peoples were the first inhabitants of what is now the United States, that they have suffered centuries of dispossession and violence, and that they continue to be vibrant, living nations deserving of recognition.

This alternative does not require anyone to abandon their Italian heritage, nor does it require that we pretend Columbus was not a real historical figure. It does not demand that we erase the history of European arrival; it demands only that we stop celebrating that arrival as a singular act of heroic discovery, and instead acknowledge the fuller, truer story: that the Americas were already inhabited, that their inhabitants built great civilizations, and that the European encounter was as much a catastrophe for them as it was a "discovery" for Europe.

Addressing Counterarguments

Defenders of Columbus Day often raise several objections that deserve direct response. The first is that "Columbus didn't know what he was starting"—that he could not have foreseen the demographic collapse, the slave trade, or the centuries of colonial exploitation. This is true in a narrow sense, but it is irrelevant to the question of whether we should celebrate him. We do not honor historical figures based on what they could not have foreseen; we honor them based on what they actually did. And what Columbus actually did, in his own lifetime, was initiate systems of enslavement, rule through terror, and engage in or order acts of violence and mutilation against Indigenous peoples who resisted him. He was even returned to Spain in chains in 1500, due to the brutality of his governance—a fact that should be as central to the historical record as his "discovery."

A second objection is that "canceling Columbus is erasing history." But the abolition of a holiday does not erase history; it changes which history a nation chooses to celebrate. Columbus will continue to be taught in schools, written about in books, and discussed in public discourse. What changes is the nation's formal expression of gratitude toward him. The history of colonization and its consequences will become more central to public consciousness, not less.

A third objection holds that "Italian-Americans need their hero." This conflates a heritage with a holiday, and ignores the diverse perspectives within Italian-American communities. Many prominent Italian-Americans, including former mayor of New York Bill de Blasio, author Don DeLillo, and numerous Italian-American scholars and activists, have supported the move to Indigenous Peoples' Day. The argument also patronizes Italian-Americans by suggesting they have no claim to American heritage unless they can claim a particular historical figure to celebrate. Italian-Americans have made immeasurable contributions to American life in every field; they do not need Columbus to validate their place in the American story.

Conclusion: A Necessary Reckoning

The abolition of Columbus Day is not an act of historical revisionism; it is an act of historical honesty. It acknowledges that the men, women, and children who were killed, enslaved, and dispossessed by Columbus and the systems he inaugurated were fully human, and that their suffering matters. It acknowledges that Indigenous peoples are not relics of a pre-Columbian past but living communities whose ancestors endured the worst of European colonization and who deserve to be recognized in the public square. It acknowledges that a nation which claims to stand for justice cannot in good conscience continue to give a federal holiday to a man whose legacy includes mutilation, enslavement, and the inauguration of one of history's greatest atrocities.

The replacement of Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day would be a small but meaningful step—a formal recognition that the story of the Americas is not a single story, and that the nation's heroes cannot include those who perpetrated genocide. Cities, states, and institutions across the country have already taken this step. The federal government should follow. To continue to honor Columbus is to participate, however unwittingly, in a long tradition of historical whitewashing. To abolish the holiday, and to replace it with one that honors Indigenous peoples, is to tell the truth about our past—and to begin to live up to the principles we claim to hold.

The question, in the end, is not whether Columbus was a complicated figure of his time. The question is what we, in our time, choose to honor—and what we choose, finally, to tell the truth about.

It costs the children of Taíno descendants, who grow up in a country that erases their ancestors from the textbooks and replaces them with a story of white triumph. It costs Indigenous students, who attend schools on land stolen from their great-grandparents, sit in classrooms built on the broken promises of a hundred treaties, and then are told in October to celebrate the man who began it all.

It costs us all. Because a nation that cannot face its history cannot heal from it. A nation that teaches its children myths will raise adults who cannot recognize injustice when they see it — because they have been trained to mistake oppression for progress.

What Indigenous Peoples Deserve

Indigenous peoples — the original inhabitants of this land, the people who fed a starving colony at Plymouth, who built the civilizations of Cahokia and Chaco Canyon, who possessed sophisticated knowledge of agriculture, astronomy, medicine, and governance long before Columbus's grandmother was born — these peoples do not need our guilt. They need our respect.

They deserve a day — not a paragraph, not a footnote, but a day — to be seen. To be honored. Not as relics of a vanished past, but as living nations: the Lakota, the Cherokee, the Navajo, the Pueblo, the Haudenosaunee, the Diné, the hundreds of distinct peoples whose sovereignty long predates any flag that flies above them.

This is why cities and states across this country are doing what Congress has not had the courage to do. They are replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day. They are not erasing history. They are correcting it. They are not attacking Italian-American heritage — a heritage that has given this nation so much and that no decent person would diminish. They are saying that we do not honor Italian heritage by clinging to a man whose own actions were monstrous. We honor Italian heritage by remembering Leonardo, by remembering Dante, by remembering the millions of Italian immigrants who came to these shores seeking the very freedom and dignity that Columbus denied to others.

A Call to Action

So here is what I ask of you — not as a favor, but as a moral duty.

Speak the truth in your homes. When your children bring home the rhyme about sailing the ocean blue, teach them the rest of the verse — the one that has been left out for too long. Teach them about the Taíno queen Anacaona. Teach them about the resistance leader Enriquillo. Teach them about the millions who died, and the millions more who survived and whose descendants walk among us today.

Demand that your schools teach honest history. Demand that your local governments follow the lead of cities that have already made the change. Demand that your representatives in Congress support legislation to replace Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day as a federal holiday.

And when you hear someone say that this is "woke revisionism" or "cancel culture" or that we are "erasing history" — ask them, plainly: Whose history are we erasing? Because the history of Indigenous peoples in this hemisphere is not taught. It is buried. It is silenced. It is not erased by people who want to teach it; it is erased by a system that never bothered to learn it in the first place.

A Final Word

We are told that America is a nation of ideals. Let us, for once, live up to them. Let us acknowledge that the wealth of this nation was built not only on the labor of the enslaved but on the dispossession of the original peoples of this land. Let us acknowledge that honoring Columbus is not a neutral act — it is a declaration that exploration and "progress" justify any atrocity.

Let us replace the lie with the truth. Let us replace the celebration of a conqueror with a celebration of the people who were here before him, who are here now, and whose survival, resilience, and contribution to this nation is the most remarkable story in the history of this continent.

This is not about tearing down. This is about building up. This is about building a country that can look at its reflection without flinching. This is about building a country worthy of the name it has claimed for itself — a country of liberty and justice, not just for some, but for all.

Thank you. And may we have the courage, finally, to do what is right.

Title: Reckoning with History: The Case for Abolishing Columbus Day

Introduction

Every October, the United States commemorates Columbus Day, a federal holiday honoring Christopher Columbus’s 1492 voyage to the Americas. However, growing national discourse reveals a stark divide. While traditionally celebrated as a symbol of exploration and Italian-American heritage, this holiday perpetuates a mythologized narrative that ignores the devastating consequences of Columbus’s expeditions on Indigenous peoples. Christopher Columbus’s legacy is not one of heroism but of colonialism, genocide, and exploitation, making the continued observance of this holiday deeply problematic. Abolishing Columbus Day is imperative to honor historical truth and acknowledge the enduring trauma inflicted on Indigenous communities. Replacing it with a day recognizing Indigenous Peoples’ heritage would foster a more equitable and accurate understanding of American history.

Body Paragraph 1: Colonialism and Displacement

Christopher Columbus’s voyages marked the beginning of European colonialism in the Americas, a system that prioritized exploitation and displacement over Indigenous sovereignty. Upon arriving in the Caribbean, Columbus and his successors quickly established colonies under Spanish authority, systematically seizing land and resources. The Spanish encomienda system, implemented shortly after his death, mandated Indigenous labor and tribute to European settlers, fundamentally restructuring societies into patriarchal, extractive economies. This system of colonial governance, rooted in the principles Columbus initiated, displaced millions of Indigenous people, eroded their cultural practices, and imposed alien governance structures. Recognizing this legacy as a basis for celebration obscures the violent foundations of territorial conquest, reinforcing a narrative that glorifies oppression rather than commemorating historical harm.

Body Paragraph 2: Genocide and Demographic Collapse

The demographic collapse of Indigenous populations in the Americas constitutes one of history’s greatest tragedies, with Columbus’s expeditions serving as a catalyst. Within decades of European contact, diseases like smallpox decimated communities already destabilized by warfare and enslavement. Historian David Stannard estimates that up to 100 million Indigenous peoples perished, a catastrophe exacerbated by Columbus’s policies. His journal entries reveal an insatiable appetite for gold and human labor, leading to brutal practices such as the enslavement of Taíno populations, who were forced to mine gold under horrific conditions. Bartolomé de las Casas, a contemporary witness, documented mass hangings and mutilations of Indigenous peoples, describing Columbus’s regime as “cruel and inhuman.” To celebrate this figure is to ignore the genocide that followed in his wake, transforming the Americas into a graveyard of civilizations.

Body Paragraph 3: Exploitation of Resources and Labor

Columbus’s arrival ushered in centuries of resource extraction and exploitative labor systems targeting Indigenous peoples. His expeditions prioritized Spanish economic interests, transforming Indigenous lands into sites of mining, agriculture, and trade that enriched Europe while impoverishing Native communities. The encomienda system, institutionalized under his successors, legally compelled Indigenous peoples into servitude, a practice defended by Columbus in his advocacy for the “subjugation of the Indians.” This exploitation stripped Indigenous peoples of their livelihoods and autonomy, reducing them to commodities in global economies. Celebrating Columbus Day celebrates the inception of these exploitative frameworks, which laid the groundwork for ongoing inequalities in land rights and economic justice.

Body Paragraph 4: Modern Implications and the Holiday’s Impact

Maintaining Columbus Day as a federal holiday perpetuates a sanitized narrative that erases Indigenous voices and experiences. For Indigenous communities, this observance symbolizes centuries of systemic erasure and violence, contributing to psychological harm and intergenerational trauma. In contrast, movements advocating for Indigenous Peoples’ Day—such as those in cities like Seattle and states like Alaska—highlight the contributions and resilience of Native peoples, fostering reconciliation and cultural recognition. The traditional “discovery” narrative is itself a myth, overlooking millennia of Indigenous societies with sophisticated governance, agriculture, and art. By honoring Columbus, the U.S. government reinforces colonial perspectives, prioritizing European achievement over Indigenous survival and innovation.

Conclusion

The time has come to reevaluate the historical figures we venerate. Christopher Columbus, far from embodying heroism, represents the violent initiation of colonialism and its genocidal legacy. Abolishing Columbus Day is not an erasure of history but a correction that acknowledges the full scope of Indigenous suffering and the ongoing struggles against systemic inequities. Substituting this holiday with Indigenous Peoples’ Day would honor the contributions of Native communities and promote a more inclusive narrative. By doing so, the United States can begin to dismantle the mythologized history that has long shielded injustice and embrace a path toward healing and justice for all. It is a moral imperative to stop celebrating oppression and instead champion the resilience and humanity of those who have endured it.

Advocates emphasize that Indigenous Peoples’ Day does not reject all European history, but seeks to rectify the uncritical veneration of figures like Columbus.

Title: The Case for Abolishing Columbus Day: A Call to Reckon with Our Past

Introduction

Christopher Columbus Day, observed annually on the second Monday of October, commemorates the arrival of Christopher Columbus in the Americas in 1492. However, a growing body of historical evidence and ethical considerations suggest that the holiday should be abolished. This essay argues that Columbus's legacy is primarily one of colonialism, genocide, and exploitation of Indigenous peoples, making it inappropriate to celebrate his actions.

Columbus's Legacy: Colonialism and Genocide

Christopher Columbus's arrival in the Americas marked the beginning of a wave of European colonization that led to the decimation of Indigenous populations. The Spanish conquistadors, under Columbus's leadership, brought with them diseases, violence, and forced labor, leading to the deaths of millions of Indigenous peoples. According to historian David Stannard, "The Spanish conquest of the Americas was a catastrophe of unimaginable proportions, a holocaust that forever changed the course of world history" (Stannard, 1992).

Columbus himself wrote in his journal about the Indigenous peoples he encountered: "They are good to be ordered about, to work and sow, and do all that is necessary, and they have good understanding. They are not like the people of the West, who are not subject to any law or government" (Columbus, 1492). This attitude of superiority and entitlement laid the groundwork for the colonialist policies that followed, leading to the systematic oppression and exploitation of Indigenous peoples.

Exploitation and Cultural Erasure

Columbus's expeditions also marked the beginning of the transatlantic slave trade, which brought millions of Africans to the Americas as slaves. This trade was a direct result of the desire for labor and resources that Columbus and his contemporaries saw in the New World. The exploitation of both Indigenous and African peoples was a fundamental aspect of the colonial enterprise.

Moreover, the celebration of Columbus Day contributes to the erasure of Indigenous cultures and histories. By focusing on the "discovery" of the Americas, the holiday marginalizes the rich and diverse cultures that had already been thriving in the region for thousands of years. This cultural erasure is a form of violence that continues to this day.

Ethical Considerations

The celebration of Columbus Day raises significant ethical questions. It is morally problematic to honor a figure whose actions led to the suffering and death of millions of people. Furthermore, the holiday perpetuates a narrative of European superiority and Indigenous inferiority, which has been used to justify ongoing discrimination and inequality.

In contrast, many Indigenous communities and their allies have advocated for a more accurate and respectful representation of history. Some have proposed replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day, a holiday that recognizes the contributions and resilience of Indigenous peoples and their ongoing struggle for justice and self-determination.

Conclusion

The legacy of Christopher Columbus is one of colonialism, genocide, and exploitation. Celebrating Columbus Day is incompatible with a commitment to justice, equality, and the truthful reckoning of history. It is time to abolish Columbus Day and replace it with a holiday that honors the resilience and contributions of Indigenous peoples.

The movement to abolish Columbus Day is gaining traction, with cities and states across the United States considering or implementing changes. By joining this movement, we can take a step towards a more just and truthful understanding of our past, and a more inclusive and respectful future.

  • Stannard, David E. (1992). American Holocaust: The Conquest of the New World. Oxford University Press.
