For generations, schoolchildren were taught a sanitized narrative: a brave explorer who "discovered" a New World, proving the earth was round and opening the door to progress. This narrative, while deeply embedded in American culture, is fundamentally misleading. When we examine the historical record with honesty and moral clarity, Christopher Columbus's legacy reveals itself to be one defined not by discovery or heroism, but by colonialism, genocide, enslavement, and exploitation. The continued observance of a federal holiday in his name is an affront to Indigenous peoples, a distortion of history, and an obstacle to genuine reconciliation. It is time — well past time — for the United States to abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday and replace it with a more honest and inclusive observance, such as Indigenous Peoples' Day.

I. Columbus Did Not "Discover" Anything

The very premise of Columbus Day rests on a fiction. Christopher Columbus did not "discover" the Americas in any meaningful sense of the word. The Western Hemisphere was already home to tens of millions of Indigenous people — the Taíno, the Carib, the Arawak, the Aztec, the Inca, the Maya, and hundreds of other nations and cultures with rich languages, complex societies, agricultural innovations, astronomical knowledge, and sophisticated governance systems. The Taíno people of the Caribbean, whom Columbus first encountered, had inhabited the islands for centuries. They had organized communities, cultivated crops, navigated the seas, and developed intricate spiritual traditions.

To say that Columbus "discovered" a land already populated by millions is to erase those people entirely — to declare, implicitly, that a place only matters when a European sets foot on it. This is not a neutral historical judgment. It is the foundational logic of colonialism: the assumption that Indigenous existence is invisible, irrelevant, or nonexistent until validated by European arrival. A federal holiday built on this premise perpetuates an ideology of erasure.

II. The Historical Record: Columbus as an Agent of Genocide and Enslavement

The most compelling argument against Columbus Day is not an argument about semantics or political correctness. It is an argument rooted in what Columbus actually did when he arrived in the Caribbean — and in the documented consequences of his actions.

The Taíno Genocide

When Columbus landed in the Bahamas on October 12, 1492, he encountered the Taíno people. His own journal entries reveal a man who immediately assessed these human beings in terms of their potential for exploitation. On October 12, he wrote: "They would make fine servants... With fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want."

Columbus returned to the Caribbean on his second voyage in 1493 with 17 ships and over 1,200 men, and he established the first permanent European settlement in the Americas — La Navidad, and later La Isabela — on the island of Hispaniola (present-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic). What followed was a systematic campaign of violence, enslavement, and terror against the Taíno people.

Columbus imposed a tribute system on the Taíno, requiring every person over the age of fourteen to deliver a specified quantity of gold dust every three months. Those who failed to meet the quota had their hands cut off and were left to bleed to death. When gold supplies dwindled, Columbus shifted to demanding cotton and other goods under the same brutal penalty. Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish priest who initially participated in the colonization but later became one of its most vocal critics, documented these atrocities in harrowing detail in his Historia de las Indias and his Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies. Las Casas described mass hangings, the burning of captives, the use of hunting dogs to tear Indigenous people apart, and widespread sexual enslavement of women and girls — including the trafficking of children as young as nine years old.

The population of Hispaniola tells the most damning story. Estimates vary, but scholars generally agree that the Taíno population of Hispaniola was between 250,000 and several million at the time of contact. Within fifty years, through a combination of violence, forced labor, starvation, and disease, the Taíno population was virtually annihilated. By the mid-sixteenth century, the Taíno had been functionally erased as a people. This is genocide by any reasonable historical or moral standard.

Columbus's Governance

Columbus served as governor of the territories he claimed for Spain, and his administration was so cruel that even his contemporaries were disturbed. Francisco de Bobadilla, sent by the Spanish Crown to investigate complaints about Columbus's governance, found such widespread evidence of torture, mutilation, and misrule that he had Columbus arrested and shipped back to Spain in chains in 1500. Columbus's own brothers, who served alongside him, were documented to have used brutal methods including public dismemberment to maintain control over Indigenous populations. While Columbus was eventually released by Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand, the fact that the Spanish Crown — itself no stranger to colonial exploitation — found his conduct excessive speaks volumes.

The Columbian Exchange and Its Human Cost

It is true that Columbus's voyages initiated the "Columbian Exchange" — the massive transfer of plants, animals, cultures, technologies, and diseases between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. Proponents of Columbus Day often cite this exchange as evidence of his transformative impact on world history. But transformation is not inherently good. The Columbian Exchange brought devastating diseases — smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus — to populations with no prior exposure and no immunity. These diseases killed an estimated 90% of the Indigenous population of the Americas within a century of contact. While Columbus cannot be held solely responsible for the biological consequences of contact, he was the agent who initiated and actively facilitated the colonial project that made mass death inevitable — and he did so through deliberate policies of conquest and subjugation, not through peaceful exchange.

III. The Holiday's Origins: A Product of Nativism, Not Historical Merit

Understanding when and why Columbus Day became a federal holiday further undermines the case for its continued observance.

The first large-scale Columbus Day celebration in the United States took place in 1792, organized by the Columbian Order of New York, to mark the 300th anniversary of Columbus's landing. But the push to establish Columbus Day as a national holiday gained momentum in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, driven largely by Italian-American communities who faced widespread discrimination and sought a symbol of Italian pride and belonging in American society. In 1892, President Benjamin Harrison proclaimed a one-time national observance of Columbus Day, partly in response to the lynching of 11 Italian-Americans in New Orleans in 1891 — one of the largest mass lynchings in American history. Italian-Americans, who were not yet considered "white" in the American racial hierarchy, turned to Columbus as a figure who could legitimize their claim to full American citizenship.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt proclaimed Columbus Day a national holiday in 1934, and in 1968, Congress made it a federal holiday effective in 1971.

The historical irony is profound: one marginalized group's struggle for acceptance was built on the celebration of a man who was the original agent of another group's destruction. While Italian-Americans' desire for recognition and dignity in the face of persecution is entirely understandable and sympathetic, the solution should not come at the expense of Indigenous peoples' truth and humanity. Italian-Americans have made extraordinary contributions to American life — in art, science, cuisine, law, labor, and civic life. There are countless Italian-Americans worthy of celebration whose legacies do not involve the enslavement and extermination of Indigenous peoples. A holiday honoring Italian-American heritage could easily be established without centering Columbus.

IV. The Moral Argument: What We Celebrate Reveals Who We Are

Holidays are not neutral. They are statements of values. They tell the nation — and the world — which stories matter, which people deserve honor, and which historical figures embody the ideals we aspire to. When the United States celebrates Columbus Day, it implicitly endorses the narrative that European colonization of the Americas was a triumphant, heroic enterprise — a story of brave explorers taming a "wild" and "empty" continent.

This narrative does real harm. For Indigenous peoples, Columbus Day is a annual reminder that their ancestors' suffering is still minimized, dismissed, or ignored by the nation that was built on their land and their labor. The American Indian Movement and many Indigenous advocacy organizations have long called for the abolition of Columbus Day, arguing that celebrating Columbus is equivalent to celebrating the beginning of a genocide that has never been formally acknowledged or redressed.

The psychological and social effects of this erasure are well-documented. Studies in Indigenous communities show that cultural invisibility and the glorification of colonial figures contribute to intergenerational trauma, diminished self-esteem among Indigenous youth, and a broader societal indifference to ongoing injustices faced by Native peoples — including poverty, inadequate healthcare, environmental racism, and violations of treaty rights. When a nation tells its Indigenous citizens that the man who initiated their ancestors' destruction deserves a federal holiday, it sends a clear message about whose suffering counts and whose does not.

V. The Shift Is Already Happening

The movement to abolish Columbus Day is not hypothetical. It is already well underway and gaining momentum across the United States.

As of 2024, more than 130 cities and numerous states have replaced Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day or a similar observance. States including Alaska, Vermont, Oregon, South Dakota, Maine, New Mexico, and others have formally adopted Indigenous Peoples' Day as a state holiday or day of recognition. The District of Columbia has done the same. Many universities, school districts, and institutions have followed suit.

President Biden became the first sitting U.S. president to officially proclaim Indigenous Peoples' Day in 2021, issuing a proclamation alongside — but distinct from — the traditional Columbus Day proclamation. While this was a welcome symbolic step, it stopped short of abolishing Columbus Day as a federal holiday, leaving the nation in a contradictory position: simultaneously celebrating and critiquing the same historical figure.

Internationally, the movement to reexamine Columbus's legacy is part of a broader reckoning with colonial history. In Latin America, October 12 was long celebrated as "Día de la Raza" (Day of the Race) but has increasingly been reframed. Venezuela renamed it "Day of Indigenous Resistance" in 2002. Bolivia celebrates it as "Day of Decolonization." Multiple countries have removed or toppled Columbus statues. These are not acts of historical erasure — they are acts of historical correction.

VI. "But We Shouldn't Erase History"

The most common objection to abolishing Columbus Day is that doing so constitutes "erasing history." This argument fundamentally misunderstands the distinction between history and celebration.

Abolishing a federal holiday does not erase Christopher Columbus from history. He will still be studied in schools, discussed in universities, examined in books and documentaries, and analyzed by historians. What changes is that the United States government will no longer officially honor him with a paid day off, public ceremonies, and the implicit endorsement of the nation. There is no federal holiday for Genghis Khan, Julius Caesar, or Hernán Cortés, and yet no one claims that their historical significance has been "erased."

The argument for "keeping" history is, in fact, the argument that most powerfully supports abolishing Columbus Day: keeping history means telling the truth about it. The sanitized Columbus story taught to generations of American schoolchildren — the Nina, the Pinta, the Santa Maria, the brave explorer who proved the earth was round — is itself a profound act of historical erasure. It erases the Taíno. It erases the genocide. It erases the enslavement. It erases the hands cut off, the bodies burned, the children trafficked. Abolishing Columbus Day and replacing it with Indigenous Peoples' Day is not an erasure of history. It is a commitment to remembering more of it, and to remembering it more honestly.

VII. Indigenous Peoples' Day: A Better Alternative

Replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day is not merely a symbolic gesture. It is an opportunity to fundamentally reframe the American relationship with its Indigenous peoples.

Indigenous Peoples' Day can serve as a day of education, reflection, and celebration — a day to honor the cultures, languages, histories, and ongoing contributions of Native peoples. It can be a day for truth-telling: for confronting the full scope of colonial violence, for acknowledging the broken treaties and stolen lands, and for recognizing the resilience and survival of Indigenous nations in the face of centuries of attempted erasure.

It can also be a day of action: a catalyst for policy changes that address the concrete, material injustices that Indigenous communities continue to face. These include the ongoing crisis of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls (MMIWG), the violation of tribal sovereignty, inadequate funding for the Indian Health Service, environmental destruction of sacred sites and treaty-protected lands, and the need for meaningful consultation with tribal nations on all decisions that affect them.

Celebrating Indigenous peoples rather than the man who set their destruction in motion is not a radical act. It is a moral minimum.

Conclusion

The case against Columbus Day is not a case for political correctness. It is a case for historical accuracy, moral consistency, and basic human decency. Christopher Columbus was not a hero who discovered a new world. He was a colonial agent who initiated a process of genocide, enslavement, and cultural destruction that devastated Indigenous populations across the Western Hemisphere. Celebrating him with a federal holiday honors not courage but conquest, not discovery but devastation.

The United States cannot credibly claim to value truth, justice, or the dignity of all people while maintaining a holiday that glorifies one of history's most destructive colonial figures. Abolishing Columbus Day and replacing it with Indigenous Peoples' Day would be an act of moral and historical honesty — a step, however modest, toward the kind of reckoning that genuine reconciliation requires.

History is not erased by telling the truth about it. It is honored.

The abolition of Columbus Day is not an attack on Italian-American heritage, nor is it an attempt to punish a historical figure by modern standards. It is a recognition that some truths are more important than comfortable myths, and that the stories a nation tells about itself shape the future it builds. We owe the next generation — all of them — a story that does not begin with a lie.

Reconsidering Columbus Day: A Case for Abolition

For decades, the second Monday of October has been set aside to honor Christopher Columbus, the Italian explorer celebrated for "discovering" America. Yet as historical scholarship has matured and the voices of Indigenous peoples have gained long-overdue attention, the justification for this federal holiday has grown increasingly untenable. A clear-eyed examination of Columbus's actions and their consequences reveals a legacy defined not by heroic discovery, but by conquest, brutality, and the devastation of Native populations. For these reasons, Columbus Day should be abolished as a federal holiday.

The Myth of Discovery

The foundational premise of Columbus Day—that Columbus "discovered" America—is itself fundamentally flawed. The Western Hemisphere was home to tens of millions of people living in complex societies long before 1492. To celebrate a "discovery" is to erase these civilizations and to adopt a Eurocentric framework that treats Indigenous existence as inconsequential until validated by European contact. Furthermore, Columbus never even set foot on the North American mainland; his voyages reached the Caribbean and parts of Central and South America. The holiday rests on a historical inaccuracy that diminishes the humanity and history of millions.

A Documented Record of Brutality

Perhaps the most compelling argument against celebrating Columbus comes from the historical record—much of it from Columbus's own writings and those of his contemporaries. Upon encountering the peaceful Taíno people, Columbus immediately assessed their potential for subjugation. In his journal, he noted that they would make excellent servants and that with a small force he could "subjugate them all."

What followed was systematic exploitation. Columbus instituted brutal labor systems in which the Taíno were forced to mine gold under threat of mutilation and death. Those who failed to meet quotas had their hands severed. He oversaw and enabled the enslavement of thousands of Indigenous people, shipping many to Europe where most died in transit. Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish priest who witnessed these events firsthand, documented atrocities so severe that he described the destruction of entire populations. Such accounts come not from modern revisionists but from observers of the era.

The Scale of Catastrophe

The consequences of Columbus's arrival extended far beyond his personal cruelties. His voyages initiated an era of colonization that brought disease, warfare, enslavement, and displacement to Indigenous peoples across the hemisphere. The Taíno population of Hispaniola, estimated in the hundreds of thousands or more, was nearly annihilated within a few generations. While some deaths resulted from diseases to which Native peoples had no immunity, this does not absolve the deliberate violence, forced labor, and policies of subjugation that Columbus personally directed. To celebrate the man who opened this chapter is to honor the beginning of one of history's great human catastrophes.

Honoring a Person Versus Acknowledging History

Defenders of the holiday sometimes argue that we should not judge historical figures by modern standards. Yet Columbus was condemned even in his own time—he was arrested and stripped of his governorship partly due to reports of his tyrannical rule. Moreover, a federal holiday is not a neutral acknowledgment of history; it is an affirmative endorsement and celebration. We can and should study Columbus as a historical figure without elevating him to the status of a national hero whose memory the entire nation is asked to honor.

A Question of Whom We Choose to Honor

Federal holidays reflect a nation's values and the figures it deems worthy of collective reverence. By continuing to honor Columbus, the United States sends a message that the suffering of Indigenous peoples is secondary to a romanticized narrative of exploration. This is particularly painful for Native American communities, for whom the holiday represents a celebration of the very forces that nearly destroyed them. Replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day—as many states and cities have already done—offers an opportunity to honor the resilience, cultures, and contributions of the peoples who were here first and who endured the consequences of colonization.

Conclusion

Abolishing Columbus Day is not an attempt to erase history; rather, it is a call to confront history honestly. Christopher Columbus's legacy is inextricably bound to colonialism, enslavement, and the devastation of Indigenous societies. A nation that aspires to justice should not enshrine such a legacy in its calendar of celebration. By abolishing Columbus Day, the United States can take a meaningful step toward acknowledging the full truth of its founding and toward honoring those whose suffering has too long been overlooked.

Abolishing Columbus Day: A Necessary Reckoning with Colonialism, Genocide, and Exploitation

In 1492, Christopher Columbus arrived in the Americas, an event long mythologized as a triumphant "discovery" of a new world. Colonialism: The Foundation of Oppression

Columbus did not "discover" the Americas; he initiated their violent colonization. Upon arrival, he claimed the lands and peoples he encountered for Spain under the Doctrine of Discovery, a racist and legally dubious principle that justified the seizure of non-Christian lands. This ideology laid the groundwork for centuries of European domination, during which Indigenous nations were forcibly displaced, their cultures suppressed, and their sovereignty denied. The encomienda system, established by Columbus, institutionalized the exploitation of Indigenous peoples by granting Spanish colonists the right to demand tribute and forced labor from them in exchange for "protection" and Christian conversion. In practice, this was little more than chattel slavery, with Indigenous people worked to death in gold mines, on plantations, and in other brutal conditions.

The consequences of this colonialism were not merely historical—they persist today. A nation that prides itself on democracy and justice cannot in good conscience continue to honor a man whose actions set in motion a system of domination that Indigenous peoples still resist.

The scale of Indigenous depopulation following Columbus’s arrival was so catastrophic that scholars increasingly describe it as genocide. It was actively facilitated by policies of violence, forced displacement, and systematic starvation.

Columbus himself was directly complicit in these atrocities. In his own writings, he boasted of his brutal tactics to subdue the Taíno people of the Caribbean. In one infamous account, he ordered the hanging of 13 Taíno leaders who resisted Spanish demands for tribute. Firstly, the narrative of Columbus as a hero and discoverer is largely a fabrication. Indigenous peoples had already inhabited the Americas for thousands of years before Columbus's arrival. They had developed complex societies, cultures, and technologies, challenging the notion of a "New World" waiting to be discovered (Mann, 2011). Columbus's arrival marked the beginning of a catastrophic era for these Indigenous populations, with dramatic declines in population due to disease, warfare, and forced labor (Thornton, 1990).

Secondly, Columbus's treatment of Indigenous peoples was marked by brutal colonialism and exploitation. He and his men exploited the native populations, enslaving them to work in mines and on plantations. In his journal, Columbus described the natives as "good to be ordered about, to work and sow, and do all that is necessary" (Columbus, 1492). The enslavement and forced labor of Indigenous peoples laid the foundation for the transatlantic slave trade, which would become a dark chapter in human history (Glick, 2014).

Thirdly, under Columbus's leadership, the Spanish imposed a system of tribute on the Taínos, the Indigenous people of Hispaniola, requiring them to pay a quota of gold every three months. If they failed to meet this quota, their hands were amputated by Spanish soldiers (Zinn, 1980). Columbus himself wrote in his journal, "A hundred castellanoes are as easily obtained for a woman as for a farm, and it is very general and there are plenty of dealings of this kind" (Columbus, 1496), referring to the trade in enslaved Indigenous women.

Moreover, the celebration of Columbus Day has historically been used to marginalize and erase the experiences and contributions of Indigenous peoples. The holiday has been marked by protests and calls for recognition of the true history of the Americas. Furthermore, the abolition of Columbus Day as a federal holiday would not be a radical departure. In 1971, South Dakota changed Columbus Day to Native American Day, and several other states have since followed suit (NMAI, 2019). This shift reflects a growing awareness and acknowledgment of the need to honor the Indigenous peoples of the Americas.

In conclusion, the legacy of Christopher Columbus is one of colonialism, genocide, and exploitation. The celebration of Columbus Day overlooks these atrocities and perpetuates a myth that disregards the true history of the Americas. It is time for a change. The abolition of Columbus Day as a federal holiday would be a step towards recognizing and honoring the Indigenous peoples of this continent, acknowledging their histories, cultures, and contributions.
